facts.statement: The researchers created a laboratory test using cell cultures from the dorsal root ganglion and microglia to see what signals cause immune cells to move.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: When dorsal root ganglion cells were grown together with microglia, the immune cells moved more than usual, showing that the ganglion cells released signals that attract them.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The substance ATP, which is found in the signals released by the dorsal root ganglion, strongly encouraged the microglia to migrate.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Two different drugs designed to block the receptors for ATP worked differently: one only stopped some of the movement, while the other did not stop it at all.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Common pain-related chemicals like CGRP, substance P, and glutamate did not cause the microglia to move when tested at normal levels, suggesting other unknown signals are responsible.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The authors state that this new laboratory method offers a useful way to study how nerve cells and immune cells talk to each other in both healthy and sick states.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue
